artifacts.synopsis: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.

artifacts.synopsis: Ryan Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its refusal to commence process against Greg Johnson on four allegations concerning same-sex attraction as sin, identity in Christ, sanctification, and fitness for office. The SJC denied the complaint in full. It found no clear procedural error and held that Johnson’s explanations and clarifications made Presbytery’s non-indictment judgments reasonable. No trial was ordered. The ruling neither adjudged Johnson guilty nor endorsed every statement or broader constitutional position concerning same-sex attraction.

artifacts.title: Dodson et al. v. Ohio Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

artifacts.synopsis: A minister appealed a judgment finding him guilty on most charges and imposing six months’ suspension. The SJC held BCO 32-20 barred Specifications 1, 2, and 4 because Presbytery lacked extraordinary justification for prosecuting old allegations, but did not bar ongoing Specification 3. It separately found the entire process constitutionally flawed and prejudicial. The SJC reversed the whole censure, declined Presbytery’s requested harsher sentence, and concluded the matter. A concurrence disputed the majority’s BCO 32-20 interpretation while agreeing with the result.

artifacts.title: Marusich v. Central Indiana Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Marusich challenged Presbytery’s receipt of a commission’s finding that accusations against a teaching elder did not establish a strong presumption of guilt, and the commission’s failure to provide minutes or a full report. Without answering either issue or identifying an error, the SJC remanded for a new BCO 31-2 investigation, a narrative of the evidence, and a recommendation for Presbytery’s consideration under regular orders. The decision expressly establishes no general rule for BCO 31-2 investigations.

artifacts.synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions and censures arising from his brief refusal to leave a closed Temporary Session meeting. The SJC affirmed only his conviction for failing to submit to church government, because he knowingly attended and his apology acknowledged fault; it reversed findings of dereliction, sedition, rioting, and the balance for lack of supporting evidence. It rejected his first four appeal specifications, but held suspension and deposition excessive, substituted Admonition, and restored both sacraments and office, although he belonged to no particular Session.

artifacts.synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

artifacts.title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

artifacts.synopsis: Teaching and ruling elders challenged Presbytery’s approval of TE Gregory Lawrence’s acquittal on five doctrinal charges. The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

Because the pivotal email was absent from the record, the SJC vacated the sabbatical-related judgment and remanded for Presbytery only to consider whether a new trial was warranted. It reversed and dismissed the clerk-duty specification because the four-month delay in submitting minutes was attributable to the Session and did not justify a trial. artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied RE Gerald Hedman's complaint against Pacific Northwest Presbytery, which had adopted five not-guilty judgments on charges that TE Peter Leithart's baptism, covenant, imputation, justification, and union-with-Christ views contradicted the Westminster Standards. Bound to the record and clear-error review, the SJC found no procedural violation and insufficient evidence that Presbytery clearly erred. It left the verdicts undisturbed, declined to endorse Leithart's views generally, and urged continued clarification of his non-standard terminology. A separate dissent would have found error and ordered a new trial or reference.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied a censured husband's complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery's approval of a judicial commission report, which had upheld his session's refusal to receive his charges against his wife after she filed for civil divorce. Applying BCO 39-3.2–3.3, the SJC deferred to the lower courts' factual and discretionary findings absent clear error. It found no clear procedural error, upheld the conclusion that the wife did not sin by seeking civil protection, and invoked BCO 31-8's caution about accusations from one under censure.

artifacts.title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. It sustained the complaint, ruling that pastoral reconciliation does not displace the duty to institute judicial process, and remanded for further proceedings; it did not adjudicate Grant guilty. A concurrence agreed only in remanding to supplement the record under BCO 42-5 & 7.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied James Urish and others' complaint against Rocky Mountain Presbytery for sustaining Dan Breed's ordination exam. Breed had said women could teach Scripture to mixed adults in settings like Sunday school under session oversight, but not preach, hold elder office, or teach outside session authority. Because the Westminster Standards and BCO did not expressly resolve that view, the SJC found no clear error under BCO 39 and affirmed Presbytery's denial. A concurrence criticized Breed's exegesis of 1 Tim. 2:12 but stressed the SJC was not endorsing it.

artifacts.synopsis: A minister appealed convictions and indefinite suspension arising from conflict over Presbytery's direction that he resign. The SJC upheld all three convictions, finding two procedural errors nonprejudicial and rejecting the other preserved challenges. But Presbytery could not treat its authority to dissolve a pastoral relationship as authority to compel resignation on pain of discipline. The SJC therefore vacated the censure and dissolution of the call and remanded for reconsideration of censure; Grady's separate administrative suspension remained effective.

artifacts.synopsis: An appeal challenged a presbytery's conviction of a minister for divisive behavior and its indefinite suspension from office and the sacraments. The SJC affirmed: the charge was lawful because publicly publishing disagreement with the session after it acted violated his ordination vows to subjection and peace/unity, even though “divisive” is not a constitutional term; the censure was not unjust absent repentance; procedural errors did not require reversal or remand. A dissent argued the charge failed BCO 29-1’s Scripture-proof requirement.

artifacts.synopsis: Westminster Presbytery was found to have erred in its BCO 31-2 investigation of secret taping by TE Frank Smith by failing to obtain full witness testimony and investigate legal ramifications; case remanded. The court found no proof of partiality and declined to require establishment of unbiblical criteria for secret taping. Vote: 18 concurring, 1 dissenting (RE Frederick Neikirk), 2 recused, 1 abstained, 2 absent.

artifacts.title: Merriam v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The SJC denied TE Stuart H. Merriam's appeal from Tennessee Valley Presbytery's April 20, 2002 conviction on three ordination-vow specifications and its indefinite suspension. It rejected procedural challenges—that the earlier called meeting was improperly convened and that TVP was prejudiced by prior cases—and found no clear error, applying BCO 39-3(2)'s deference to lower-court factual findings. The SJC sustained TVP's judgment; prior SJC Cases 95-10 and 96-7 had only indirect bearing and did not require retrial.

artifacts.synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

artifacts.synopsis: The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.
